research.title: Which algorithm predicts teen spending best?
research.intro: CoinFlow forecasts how much you will spend this week. Before choosing the method, we tested five classic forecasting algorithms in a reproducible experiment.
research.question: Can a simple algorithm that runs on the phone predict next week's spending accurately, and does modelling the trend (Holt's method) beat a simple moving average?
research.design: {ledgers} synthetic teen ledgers (26 weeks each, 5 spending profiles), rolling-origin evaluation, {forecasts} forecasts per method, Wilcoxon signed-rank test (α = 0.05).
research.h1: Holt's trend method is more accurate than the 4-week moving average. Result: it was 24.5 % less accurate (p < 0.001), even on ledgers with a trend.
research.h2: Every smoothing method beats the naive “same as last week” forecast. Result: true for all three (p < 0.01).
research.chartSubtitle: Mean absolute error in lei per week (lower is better). DAMPED was added after the main experiment.
research.tableNote: Bold = lowest error for that profile.
research.sensitivitySubtitle: Rising-trend ledgers with less and less day-to-day noise. The gap shrinks, but the moving average stays best.
research.conclusion: On short, noisy teen spending data, simpler is better: the 4-week moving average had the lowest error, and the more complex trend methods overreacted to random spikes. Damping the trend (Gardner & McKenzie) reduced Holt's error by about 10 % but did not beat the moving average.
research.inApp: That is why CoinFlow's weekly forecast uses the 4-week moving average.
research.reproduce: Code and data to repeat the experiment
